what: Two freely hinged arms rotate with a motor-driven crossbar. Higher speed makes them swing outward against gravity. Free arms swing outward as the rotor speeds up. Compare angular speed squared with gravity; reverse and compare again.
try: Reset and run the three speed stages. Compare the average arm tilt while allowing for oscillation.
Watch the arms swing after the rotor stops.
Compare forward and reverse rotation at the middle speed.
why: A rotating arm needs centripetal acceleration. In the rotating frame its outward inertial effect competes with gravity. The speed enters squared. This is a governor mechanism demonstrator; the arms do not automatically regulate the motor.
matters: Mechanical governors use this speed-sensitive motion as part of a feedback linkage.
question: At equal speed magnitude, should reversing rotation pull the arms inward instead?
answer: No. The centrifugal term depends on angular speed squared. Forward and reverse have the same ideal steady equilibrium; transitions and oscillations can differ.
further: Compare a doubled low speed with the change in mean tilt.
A real distributed arm is not a point mass: use the simple formula as an approximation.
formula: point-mass approximation: tan(tilt) ≈ ω² × radius / g
